lines.text: Spawn a real child process with a real process builder.
Does it get its own, separate process identifier, or does it somehow share the parent's?
It gets its own, completely separate identifier.
Spawning genuinely forks and execs a distinct process — not merely a distinct name for the same one.
Run it for real: the spawned child had its own, genuinely different process identifier.
And its real exit code was observed exactly, round-tripped straight back through a completely separate process.
A process already running several real threads calls a real fork.
How many threads does the resulting child actually have?
Exactly one — the single thread that called fork.
The entire address space gets copied, every byte of it, but only one thread is there to run it afterward.

lines.text: Run it for real: the parent genuinely had several real threads running, and the forked child had exactly one.
Which is exactly why only a narrow, carefully safe set of operations are allowed there before that child execs.
Send a signal through a stable process handle, to a process that has already exited and been properly reaped.
Does it silently succeed, silently fail, or fail with a specific, clear error?
It fails with a clear, specific error.
That handle never confuses a process that's genuinely gone with some other one that happens to share an old number.
Run it for real: sending through that handle succeeded while the real process was still alive.
And it failed outright, with that exact clear error, the instant the process was genuinely gone — never silently reaching anything else.
Why did setting an environment variable become unsafe to call directly, when it was perfectly fine to call for years before?
What actually changed?
Because it genuinely races with a C function that reads the environment.
And no library anywhere can be relied on to never call that function internally, without ever telling anyone.
That function's own safety section says it plainly: sound alone on a single thread, or on one particular operating system.
Everywhere else, in a multithreaded program, the only genuinely sound choice is simply never to call it at all.

lines.text: So, pulling this together: every one of these rules is really the same rule, said three separate ways.
A forked child, a stable process handle, and a shared global variable are each state that something else might be touching at that exact same moment.
So, pulling this topic together: spawning a child genuinely gives it its own, separate identity, never the parent's.
A forked child genuinely runs with only one thread, the very one that called fork, and nothing else survives there.
And a stable handle to a process never, ever gets confused with some unrelated process that happens to share an old number.
